la:verb:accuso.html:
ac-cūso (also with ss; cf. P.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
fr. causa; cf. cludo with claudo
, orig. = ad causam provocare,
to call one to account, to make complaint against, to reproach, blame.
In gen., of persons: si id non me accusas, tu ipse objurgandus es,if you do not call me to account for it, you yourself deserve to be reprimanded,: quid me accusas?: meretricem hanc primum adeundam censeo, oremus, accusemus gravius, denique minitemur,we must entreat, severely chide, and finally threaten her,: ambo accusandi,you both deserve reproach,: cotidie accusabam,I daily took him to task,: me accusas cum hunc casum tam graviter feram,; Manut.: me tibi excuso in eo ipso, in quo te accuso,: ut me accusare de epistularum neglegentia possis,that you may blame me for my tardiness in writing,. —Also metaph. of things, to blame, find fault with: alicujus desperationem,: inertiam adolescentium, id. de Or. 1, 58 (cf. incusare, ); hence also: culpam alicujus,to lay the fault on one,; cf. ; ; .—Hence,
Esp.
Transferred to civil life, to call one to account publicly (ad causam publicam, or publice dicendam provocare), to accuse, to inform against, arraign, indict (while incusare means to involve or entangle one in a cause); t. t. in Roman judicial lang.; constr. with aliquem alicujus rei (like κατηγορεῖν, cf. P.): accusant ii, qui in fortunas hujus invaserunt, causam dicit is, cui nihil reliquerunt,: numquam, si se ambitu commaculasset, ambitus alterum accusaret,: ne quis ante actarum rerum accusaretur,that no one should be called to account for previous offences,; Milt. 1, 7. Other rarer constructions are: aliquem aliquid (only with id, illud, quod), ; cf. : aliquo crimine,; ; ; : de pecuniis repetundis,; cf.: de veneficiis,: inter sicarios,; cf. Zumpt, § 446; Rudd. 2, 165 sq.; 169, note 4.—The punishment that is implied in the accusation is put in gen.: capitis,to accuse one of a capital crime,; cf. Zumpt, § 447. —
Casus accusandi, the fourth case in grammar, the accusative case, Var. L. L. 8, § 66 Müll.; v. accusativus.

la:verb:accipio.html:
ac-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3, v. a. (
fut. perf. accepso = accepero, Pac. ap. , or R) [capio], to accept.
In gen., to take a person or thing to one's self: leno ad se accipiet hominem et aurum, will take the man and his money to himself (into his house), .
Of things received by the hand, to take, receive: cette manus vestras measque accipite, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 320 ed. Vahl.): ex tua accepi manu pateram,; hence, trop. of the word given, the promise, with which a grasping of the hand was usually connected: accipe daque fidem, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 33 ed. Vahl.; so in the Gr. πιστὰ δοῦναι καὶ λαβεῖν); cf. ; so ; in Ter. of a person to be protected: hanc (virginem) accepi, acceptam servabo,; cf. , and , —
Of things received or taken by different parts of the body: accipite hoc onus in vestros collos, Cato ap. : gremio,: oculis aut pectore noctem (i. e. somnum),.—
In gen., very freq.,
as implying action, to take, to take possession of, to accept (Gr. δέχεσθαι);
of something that falls to one's share, to get, to receive, to be the recipient of (Gr. λαμβάνειν).—
To take, accept: hanc epistulam accipe a me,take this letter from me,; ; cf. : persuasit aliis, ut pecuniam accipere mallent,: condicionem pacis,: armis obsidibusque acceptis Crassus profectus est,after he had taken into his possession the arms and hostages,: divitias,: aliquid a patre,to inherit,; : accipe et haec, manuum tibi quae monumenta mearum sint,—Hence to receive or entertain as guest: haec (tellus) fessos placidissima portu accipit,: Laurentes nymphae, accipite Aenean,; 155; —Of admittance to political privileges: Nomentani et Pedani in civitatem accepti,; cf. : magnifice volo summos viros accipere,: in loco festivo sumus festive accepti,; so ; ; , etc.; ; ; ; —Hence also ironically, to entertain, to treat, deal with: ego te miseris jam accipiam modis,: hominem accipiam quibus dictis maeret,: indignis acceptus modis,. Perh. also Lucil. ap. : adeo male me accipiunt decimae, treat or use me ill, deal harshly with me; and : sic, inquam, veteratorem illum vetulum lupum Hannibalem acceptum (Non. explains the latter in a very unusual manner, by deceptum).—
To get, to receive, to be the recipient of, Pac. ap. ; ; : ictus, (cf. : vulnera accipiunt tergo): aridior nubes accipit ignem, takes or catches fire, ; : humanitatem iis tribuere debemus, a quibus accepimus,: pecuniam ob rem judicandam,: luna lumen solis accipit,; cf. : praeclarum accepimus a majoribus morem,: praecepta, Caes. B. G. 2, 6: accepi tuas litteras (in another sense than above), I have received your letter, it has reached me (allatae sunt ad me), ; ; : acceptā injuriā ignoscere quam persequi malebant,; : calamitatem,: detrimenta,; cf. So often of dignities and offices: provinciam,: consulatum,: Galliam,
In partic.
To take a thing by hearing, i. e.,
To hear, to perceive, to observe, to learn (cf. opp. do = I give in words, i. e. I say): hoc simul accipe dictum, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 204): quod ego inaudivi, accipite, Pac. ap. (R): hoc etiam accipe quod dico, Lucil. ap. : carmen auribus, (so ); 1, 270; cf. : voces, (so 6, 171): si te aequo animo ferre accipiet,: quae gerantur, accipies ex Pollione,; ; . —Hence very freq. in the histt., to get or receive intelligence of any thing, to learn: urbem Romam, sicuti ego accepi, condidere atque habuere initio Trojani,as I have learned,, and so al.—
To comprehend or understand any thing communicated: haud satis meo corde accepi querelas tuas,: et si quis est, qui haec putet arte accipi posse,: ut non solum celeriter acciperet, quae tradebantur, etc.,; so ; —
With the accessory idea of judging, to take a thing thus or thus, to interpret or explain, usually constr. with ad or in c. acc.: quibus res sunt minus secundae . . . ad contumeliam omnia accipiunt magis,the more unfortunate one is, the more inclined is he to regard every thing as an insult,: in eam partem accipio,; cf. ; ; : non recte accipis,you put a wrong construction upon this,: quae sibi quisque facilia factu putat, aequo animo accipit,.— Hence: accipere aliquid omen, or in omen, to regard a thing as a (favorable) omen, to accept the omen (cf. δέχεσθαι τὸν οἰωνόν), ; ; ; fin.; ; ; ; —Hence poet.: accipio agnoscoque deos,; cf. .—
To take a thing upon one's self, to undertake (syn. suscipio): accipito hanc ad te litem,: meā causā causam accipite, alt. prol. 47; cf. ; so ; —Hence also,
To bear, endure, suffer any thing disagreeable or troublesome: hanccine ego ut contumeliam tam insignem ad me accipiam!: nil satis firmi video, quamobrem accipere hunc me expediat metum,; ; ; ; ; : calamitatem,: injuriam, al.—
To accept a thing, to be satisfied with, to approve: dos, Pamphile, est decem talenta; Pam.: Accipio,: accepit condicionem, dein quaestum accipit,: visa ista ... accipio iisque interdum etiam assentior, nec percipio tamen,: preces suas acceptas ab dis immortalibus ominati, Drak. Cf. Herz, : equi te esse feri similem, dico. Ridemus et ipse Messius: accipio.I allow it, Exactly so, .—
In mercant. lang., t. t., to receive or collect a sum: pro quo (frumento) cum a Varinio praetore pecuniam accepisset,; hence subst.: acceptum, i, n., the receipt, and in account-books the credit side: in acceptum referre alicui,to carry over to the credit side, to place to one's credit,; ; ; ; (opp. datum or expensum).—Hence also trop., to owe or be indebted to one, in a good or a bad sense: ut esset nemo qui non mihi vitam suam, liberos, remp. referret acceptam,: omnia mala, quae postea vidimus, uni accepta referemus Antonio,ascribe,; ; id. B. C, 3, 57: Acceptum

refero versibus, esse nocens, . —

In the gram m., to take a word or phrase thus or thus, to explain a word in any manner: adversus interdum promiscue accipitur, P. al.—(Syn. nanciscor and adipiscor: he to whom something is given, accipit; he who gets by a fortunate occurrence, nanciscitur; he who obtains it by exertion, adipiscitur.Sumimus ipsi: accipimus ab alio, Vel. Long. p. 2243 P.—Inter tenere, sumere et accipere hoc interest, quod tenemus quae sunt in nostra potestate: sumimus posita: accipimus data, ).—Hence, acceptus, a, um, P. a., welcome, agreeable, acceptable (syn. gratus. Acceptus is related to gratus, as the effect to the cause; he who is gratus, i. e. dear, is on that account acceptus, welcome, acceptable; hence the usual position: gratus atque acceptus).—First, of persons: essetne apud te is servus acceptissimus?: plebi acceptus erat,; acceptus erat in oculis,.— Of things: dis et hominibus est acceptum quod, etc.,: quod vero approbaris. id gratum acceptumque habendum,: munus eorum gratum acceptumque esse,: quorum mihi dona accepta et grata habeo,: rem populo Romano gratam acceptamque,; tempore accepto exaudivi,.—Comp., ; ; —Sup., see above.—Adv.accepte does not occur.

senses: to find comfort or pleasure (in); rejoice (in); occupy oneself (in/with)
la:verb:acquiesco.html:
ac-quĭesco (adqu.), ēvi, ētum, 3, v. n., lit.,
to become physically quiet, to come to physical repose; hence, in gen., to repose or rest (freq. in Cic.).
Lit.: sine respirem, quaeso. Pe. Immo adquiesce, ; : vitandi caloris causā Lanuvii trīs horas acquieveram,: a lassitudine,: somno,; cf.: gravi sopore,, and absol. of sleep, : cum aures extremum semper exspectent in eoque acquiescant,.—By euphemism (as in all languages), to die (esp. after a wearisome life): sic vir fortissimus multis variisque perfunctus laboribus, anno acquievit septuagesimo,; cf. morte,; and in many epitaphs: HIC ADQVIESCIT, etc.,; ; ; so, quiesco, q. v.
Fig.
To come to a state of repose in relation to one's wishes, desires, etc.; to repose in; to find rest, pleasure, etc., in; to rejoice in; in Cic. mostly with in, and of things: in the historians and later writers, with dat. or abl., and also of persons: quae delectet, in qua acquiescam,: senes in adulescentium caritate acquiescimus,; : qui jam aetate provecti in nostris libris acquiescunt,. Examples in Cic. of a person: tecum ut quasi loquerer, in quo uno acquiesco,, and with abl.: qui maxime P. Clodii morte acquierunt,: cui velut oraculo acquiescebat,: uno solatio acquiescens,; : amicos elegit, quibus etiam post eum principes acquieverunt,.—
To be satisfied with, to acquiesce in or give assent to: tu, cum es commotus, acquiescis, assentiris, approbas (where the climax of the ideas should be noticed, you accede to them, i. e. you cease to oppose them; you assent to them, i. e. you make known your approbation by words), ; so ; ;

la:verb:accedo.html:
ac-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, v. n. (
perf. sync., accēstis, ), to go or come to or near, to approach (class.).
Lit.
In gen., constr. with ad, in, the local adverbs, the acc., dat., infin., or absol.
With ad: accedam ad hominem,; so, ad aedīs,: ad flammam,: omnīs ad aras,to beset every altar,: ad oppidum,: ad ludos,: ad Caesarem supplex,: ad manum, to come to their hands (of fishes), : ad Aquinum,; so, ad Heracleam,.—Impers.: ad eas (oleas) cum accederetur,.—
With in: ne in aedīs accederes,: in senatum,: in Macedoniam,: in funus aliorum,to join a funeral procession,—
With local adv.: eodem pacto, quo huc accessi, abscessero,: illo,: quo,.—
With acc. (so, except the names of localities, only in poets and historians, but not in Caesar and Livy): juvat integros accedere fontīs atque haurire,, and 4, 2: Scyllaeam rabiem scopulosque,: Sicanios portus,; cf. : Africam,: aliquem,; ; : classis Ostia cum magno commeatu accessit,: Carthaginem,.—(ε) With dat. (poet.): delubris,: silvis,: caelo (i. e. to become a god), , and 870.—(* ζ) With inf.: dum constanter accedo decerpere (rosas),—(η) Absol.: accedam atque hanc appellabo,: deici nullo modo potuisse qui non accesserit,: accessit propius,: quoties voluit blandis accedere dictis,—Impers.: non potis accedi, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 17 ed. Vahl.): quod eā proxime accedi poterat,.
In partic.
To approach a thing in a hostilemanner (like aggredior, adorior), to attack: acie instructa usque ad castra hostium accessit,: sese propediem cum magno exercitu ad urbem accessurum,: ad manum,to fight hand to hand, to engage in close combat,; : ad corpus alicujus,: Atque accedit muros Romana juventus, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 527 ed. Vahl.): hostīs accedere ventis navibus velivolis, id. ap. (Ann. v. 380 ib.); and, in malam part.,.—
Mercant. t. t.: accedere ad hastam,to attend an auction,; .—
In late Lat.: ad manus (different from ad manum, B. 1), to be admitted to kiss hands, Capit. .
Fig.
In gen., to come near to, to approach: haud invito ad aurīs sermo mi accessit,; so, clemens quidam sonus aurīs ejus accedit,: si somnus non accessit,; cf.: febris accedit,: ubi accedent anni,; cf.: accedente senectā,.
In partic.
To come to or upon one, to happen to, to befall (a meaning in which it approaches so near to accĭdo that in many passages it has been proposed to change it to the latter; cf. Ruhnk. Rut. Lup. 1, p. 3; 2, p. 96; Dictat. in and 225); constr. with ad or (more usually) with dat.: voluntas vostra si ad poëtam accesserit,: num tibi stultitia accessit?have you become a fool?: paulum vobis accessit pecuniae,: dolor accessit bonis viris, virtus non est imminuta,: quo plus sibi aetatis accederet,
With the accessory idea of increase, to be added = addi; constr. with ad or dat.: primum facie (i. e. faciei) quod honestas accedit, Lucil. ap. ; so ap. : ad virtutis summam accedere nihil potest,: Cassio animus accessit,; ; : pretium agris,the price increases, advances,.—Absol.: plura accedere debent,: accedit mors,; : quae jacerent in tenebris omnia, nisi litterarum lumen accederet, (so, not accenderet, is to be read).—If a new thought is to be added, it is expressed by accedit with quod (add to this, that, etc.) when it implies a logical reason, but with ut (beside this, it happens that, or it occurs that) when it implies an historical fact (cf. Zumpt, § 621 and 626): accedit enim, quod patrem amo,: so Cael. ap. ; ; ; ; ; ; on the other hand: huc accedit uti, etc.,: ad App. Claudii senectutem accedebat etiam ut caecus esset,; so ; ; ; ; When several new ideas are added, they are introduced by res in the plur.: cum ad has suspiciones certissimae res accederent: quod per fines Sequanorum Helvetios transduxisset; quod obsides inter eos dandos curāsset; quod ea omnia, etc.,. Sometimes the historical idea follows accedit, without ut: ad haec mala hoc mihi accedit etiam: haec Andria ... gravida e Pamphilo est,: accedit illud: si maneo ... cadendum est in unius potestatem,.
To give assent to, accede to, assent to, to agree with, to approve of; constr. with ad or dat. (with persons only, with dat.): accessit animus ad meam sententiam,; so ; : Galba speciosiora suadentibus accessit,; so
To come near to in resemblance, to resemble, be like; with ad or dat. (the latter most freq., esp. after Cic.): homines ad Deos nulla re propius accedunt quam salutem hominibus dando,: Antonio Philippus proximus accedebat,; cf. ; ;
To enter upon, to undertake; constr. with ad or in: in eandem infamiam,: ad bellorum pericula,: ad poenam,to undertake the infliction of punishment,: ad amicitiam Caesaris,: ad vectiǵalia,to undertake their collection as contractor,: ad causam,the direction of a lawsuit,; But esp.: ad rem publicam,to enter upon the service of the state,;

While they extended the lower part of the body upon the couch (triclinium, lectus triclinaris), they supported the upper part by the left arm upon a cushion (or upon the bosom of the one nearest; hence, in sinu accumbere,; cf. ἀνακεῖσθαι = εἶναι ἐν τῷ κόλπῳ τινός, Ev. Ioh. 13, 23), the right hand only being used in taking food: hoc age, adcumbe,; so , etc.; ; ; ; c. acc.: mensam, Att. ap. ; ; : cotidianis epulis in robore,: in convivio,: in epulo,: epulis,; tecum,; absol., .—Since three persons usually reclined upon such a couch (cf. ), these expressions arose: in summo (or superiorem, also supra), medium and imum (or infra) adcumbere; and the series began on the left side, since they lay supported by the left arm. The whole arrangement is explained by the following figure: Among the three lecti, the lectus medius was the most honorable; and on each lectus, the locus medius was more honorable than the summus; and this had the preference to the imus or ultimus. The consul or other magistrate usually sat as imus of the lectus medius (fig. no. 6), in order that, by his position at the corner, he might be able, without trouble, to attend to any official business that might occur. The place no. 7 seems, for a similar reason, to have been taken by the host. See on this subject Salmas. ; Smith's Antiq.; Becker's Gall. 3, p. 206 sq. (2d ed.); and Orell. excurs. ad .
